The Market for Money

In micro, money barely showed up at all. In Keynes's macro, the money market sets the interest rate.

People like holding money because it is handy. The more nervous they feel, the more they hold. The central bank fixes how much money exists. The rate settles where the two meet, as the formulas below show. Print more money, and the rate falls.

For example, the whole class together carries a fixed pile of 💰 cash. On field-trip day everyone wants to carry more, so cash gets scarce. Scarce cash means borrowing it costs more — a higher interest rate.

L(r)=L0+kY−hrL(r) = L_0 + k Y - h rL(r)=L0​+kY−hr
r∗=L0+kY−M/Phr^* = \frac{L_0 + k Y - M/P}{h}r∗=hL0​+kY−M/P​

Examples & Exercises

The central bank raises the real money supply from M/P=90M/P = 90M/P=90 to 110110110 (income stays at Y=200Y = 200Y=200).

How far does the interest rate move?

Show proof

  1. Before, r∗=(L0+kY−M/P)/h=(40+0.5⋅200−90)/10=5r^* = (L_0 + k Y - M/P) / h = (40 + 0.5 \cdot 200 - 90) / 10 = 5r∗=(L0​+kY−M/P)/h=(40+0.5⋅200−90)/10=5. With money at 110110110, r∗=(140−110)/10=3r^* = (140 - 110) / 10 = 3r∗=(140−110)/10=3.

  2. The move is Δr=−Δ(M/P)/h=−20/10=−2\Delta r = -\Delta (M/P) / h = -20 / 10 = -2Δr=−Δ(M/P)/h=−20/10=−2 points.

    When money is plentiful, the price of borrowing it falls too — the liquidity effect.

    And at this rate the loanable-funds investment curve I=100−6rI = 100 - 6rI=100−6r points to 828282, so monetary policy reaches aggregate demand through investment.

A boom lifts income from Y=200Y = 200Y=200 to 240240240 (money stays at M/P=90M/P = 90M/P=90).

The central bank did nothing — why does the interest rate move anyway?

Show proof

  1. Higher income means more spending, and more spending means holding more money for transactions. The demand intercept rises from L0+kY=40+0.5⋅200=140L_0 + k Y = 40 + 0.5 \cdot 200 = 140L0​+kY=40+0.5⋅200=140 to 40+0.5⋅240=16040 + 0.5 \cdot 240 = 16040+0.5⋅240=160, so equilibrium is r∗=(160−90)/10=7r^* = (160 - 90) / 10 = 7r∗=(160−90)/10=7.

  2. The move is Δr=kΔY/h=0.5⋅40/10=+2\Delta r = k \Delta Y / h = 0.5 \cdot 40 / 10 = +2Δr=kΔY/h=0.5⋅40/10=+2 points. The supply of money is unchanged, but everyone wants to hold more of it, so the price of giving it up — the interest rate — has to rise.
